name: Limit of the small form action-image
definition: The small form (action reveals situation) reflects on itself until action can no longer disclose the situation: parallel, heterogeneous lines of action connect only as a 'special homogeneity', leaving the question as a sustained, unanswered ellipsis.
deamer_quote: the coordinates of a question will ultimately and necessarily be left unanswered (p. 117)
deleuze_examples: The Life of Oharu (Kenji Mizoguchi, 1952) - Deleuze's 'lines of the universe' passing through women (C1: 195)
Ugetsu (Kenji Mizoguchi, 1953)
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Three cops - Eddie, Tango, Sal - are intercut as three isolated lines that the film refuses to join.
Burned-out Eddie, a week from retirement, is saddled with a rookie ride-along whom he abandons.
The three protagonists fleetingly cross paths in one inner-city tower block, a crossing Deamer calls a ruse.
Their three outcomes read like three rolls of the dice, interchangeable between the men.

operation: Cut parallel lines of action that never meet, and let the one moment they share space explain nothing.
shot_criteria: A shot where separate figures or actions share a space without connecting (passing, facing away, split apart), or an isolated clue/fragment that resolves nothing; no convergence or payoff visible in frame.
queries: three strangers walking off in different directions across a city intersection, high angle, black and white
police patrol car parked on a night street under a streetlight, lone officer at the wheel
housing project courtyard, residents passing each other without looking, wide shot
man climbing alone up a long concrete tenement stairwell, shot from above
pair of dice tumbling across a green felt table, close up
hands trying to fit scattered jigsaw puzzle pieces on a table, overhead close up
split screen of different people talking on telephones in separate rooms
commuters crisscrossing a railway station concourse in many directions, overhead shot

name: Limit of the action-image (extreme limit)
position_detail: sign of genetic forces (Deamer's own naming; Deleuze only hints at it)
definition: Where the limits of the large and small forms converge and we can no longer tell which form is originary: action curves back toward the any-space-whatever and the film is permeated, from start to end, by problems - the universe as a cipher of indeterminate forces.
deamer_quote: A whole world of problems, puzzles, questions and ciphers. (p. 118)
deleuze_examples: Films of Akira Kurosawa (large-form limit) and Kenji Mizoguchi (small-form limit), which Deleuze says are 're-united in the notion of the any-space-whatever' (C1: 187)
Dersu Uzala (Akira Kurosawa, 1975) - taiga as problem-space
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: The Ramirez family leave the rice terraces of Benguet after being forced to sell rice at a ruinous rate.
Hand-held close-ups on Manila streets as the family are conned, lose their lodging and end in the slum; Oscar shifts rubble for a day and is cheated.
Mai works as a hostess at Charlie's while Oscar drifts into an armoured security-van job and a heist.
In the heist Oscar finds two keys: an actual one that is a ruse, and a hidden imprint, an empty void, that unlocks the future.

operation: Let two incompatible modes of the same story reflect on each other until the only thing left on screen is the problem itself.
shot_criteria: An indeterminate problem-space or cipher object: an empty/any-space-whatever setting, a maze, an imprint or absence standing for an answer, or a labour/social milieu shown as an open question rather than a plot situation.
queries: terraced rice paddies on a steep mountainside, farmers bent over working, wide shot
shantytown of tin shacks beside a river, children walking a muddy path
day laborer shoveling rubble at a demolition site, dust hanging in the air
armored security truck at curb, uniformed guards carrying money bags into a bank
key pressed into a bar of soap leaving an imprint, extreme close up
hedge maze seen from above with a small figure lost inside
empty vacant lot in fog with scattered debris and no people, static wide shot
blackboard crowded with equations and question marks, teacher pointing, black and white

name: Rich dream
position_detail: first sign of full molar composition
definition: The explicitly signalled dream: entry and exit are marked, and the dream is built from overloaded technical means - dissolves, superimpositions, deframings, special effects - so the dream world is radically distinct from the real, yet its affects carry back into waking action.
deamer_quote: This is a dream! - such is the formula of the rich dream (p. 123)
deleuze_examples: Entr'acte (René Clair, 1924)
Un chien andalou (Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, 1929)
Sherlock Jr. (Buster Keaton, 1924) - the projectionist dreams himself into the screen
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: The camera pulls back from black to reveal an eye, then a face staring into the lens, then a man in a glass tube among countless others in an impossibly vast ship.
The camera flies side to side down a corridor like a disembodied spirit.
Picard lies restrained on an operating table, his head encased in machinery; the image distorts and a drill enters his eye.
A zoom in on the sleeping Picard as he opens his eyes signals it was a dream.

operation: Mark the passage into sleep with an optical transformation and fill the dream with images only trick photography can make.
shot_criteria: A single shot visibly marked as dream by optical means: superimposition/double exposure, dissolve, distortion, trick-film impossibility, or a sleeper with dream imagery overlaid; plain realist shots do not count.
queries: sleeping man in bed with dream images superimposed above his head, double exposure, black and white
extreme close up of an eye opening, camera slowly pulling back to reveal the face
kaleidoscope trick effect of multiplied faces rotating, silent film
woman floating among stars in black space, early trick photography
face warped by rippling wavy-glass distortion effect
girl falling down a long tunnel past floating furniture, silent film
man strapped to an operating table under large machinery and bright lights, science fiction set
cartoon character asleep in bed with fantasy scene in a thought bubble above

name: Restrained dream
definition: The dream entered by a straight cut or invisible transition, resembling everyday reality but subtly impossible - an 'unhinging' between concrete objects - so that dream and real become ambiguous and the film's task becomes telling them apart.
deamer_quote: Was I asleep? Am I now awake? (p. 124)
deleuze_examples: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (Luis Buñuel, 1972) - dreams entered by straight cut
Late Buñuel generally: 'a perpetual unhinging' between concrete objects (C2: 58)
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: As Trevor's eyes close, a book slips from his hand to the floor, a cup clatters on a coffee-bar counter, a car lighter pops on the dashboard, and he is thrown awake.
The film is shot in half-light, all murky blue-greys, around an emaciated man moving slowly with blank stares.
A co-worker named Ivan at the machine shop whom nobody else has heard of.
Post-it notes with a hangman game appear on his fridge; he spends hours scrubbing the bathroom floor.

operation: Cut straight from waking to dream with no optical signal, and let one ordinary object behave slightly wrongly.
shot_criteria: An unmarked, realist shot (no superimposition or dissolve) of an everyday setting or object that reads as uncanny: a drowsing or dazed figure, dim half-light, an object isolated and oddly emphasised.
queries: man dozing off on a sofa, book slipping from his hand onto the floor
coffee cup set down on a diner counter, waitress behind it, close up
driver's hand at car dashboard cigarette lighter at night, close up
gaunt worker at a lathe in a dim machine shop, sparks flying
dark kitchen at night, refrigerator door with paper notes stuck on it
man staring blankly out a rain-streaked window in a dim room
person on hands and knees scrubbing a bathroom tile floor
lone figure standing motionless on a deserted foggy street at dawn

name: Movement of world
definition: The implied dream with no entrance and no exit: the world itself closes around everything including the dreamer, and a movement of world (song, dance, impossible events) supplants the faltering movement of the character, so dream and real are one.
deamer_quote: There is no entrance to the dream world, and no exit. (p. 125)
deleuze_examples: The Band Wagon (Vincente Minnelli, 1953)
Brigadoon (Vincente Minnelli, 1954)
Singin' in the Rain (Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly, 1952)
Top Hat (Mark Sandrich, 1935) - Astaire's dance as passage into movement of world
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Cobb's totem, a spinning top, gyrates on his kitchen table before a cut to black.
Dream cities fold: cliffs made of decaying buildings, mirrors reconstructing cityscapes, the earth curving back on itself.
Dreams nested within dreams within dreams, time stretching at each level.
The top first belonged to Mal and 'tells him nothing' - the whole film may be a dream.

operation: Make the whole world move to one impossible rhythm so that no one stands outside the dream.
shot_criteria: A shot where the setting itself moves with dreamlike or choreographed logic (dancing crowds, animated surroundings, rotating/folding world, perpetual spinning) and no dreamer frames it as a dream.
queries: spinning top whirling on a wooden kitchen table, close up
chorus line of dancers kicking in unison on a stage, wide shot
man dancing down a street as passersby fall into step with him
small children dressed in adult suits and hats staging a mock wedding
city street tilting as the camera rotates until buildings turn sideways
cartoon where trees, houses and lampposts dance to music
overhead kaleidoscope formation of synchronized swimmers in a pool
carousel turning at night with blurred lights and riders going round

name: Strong destiny
position_detail: first sign of full molar composition (Deamer's division of Deleuze's 'destiny')
definition: The marked flashback as closed circuit of psychological causality: a character pauses, a slow dissolve or shimmer leads to a signalled past, and that past returns through affect into action, determining the character's inescapable future.
deamer_quote: Strong destiny explicates the inescapable past (p. 129)
deleuze_examples: Le jour se lève (Marcel Carné, 1939) - flashbacks from the besieged room as fatal destiny
Double Indemnity (Billy Wilder, 1944) - confession frame determining the past
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

section3.film: The Secret in Their Eyes (Juan José Campanella, 2009)
scenes: Espósito, face in darkness, slowly pushes open an old wooden door and enters a hidden space.
One doorway has makeshift, bent iron bars leading to a room with a bricked-up window; another opens on a brightly lit room where Morales stands with his back turned.
Through a small opening in the improvised cell shuffles a broken, balding old man - the killer, held for 25 years.
The retired agent sets out to novelise 1974, structuring the film as present-past-present.

operation: Hold on a face in the present, dissolve slowly into a marked past, and return with that past driving the next act.
shot_criteria: One pole of a flashback circuit: a present-tense figure pausing in reverie (ideally as a dissolve begins), or a visibly 'marked' past image (soft focus, glow, monochrome, slow motion); or an object/space from the past confronted in the present.
queries: old man in armchair gazing into the distance, slow dissolve into a younger scene
hand pushing open an old wooden door into a dark room, silhouetted figure entering
gaunt old prisoner behind a small window of bent iron bars
man at a typewriter at night under a lamp, pausing and looking up
hand holding a faded family photograph, extreme close up
courtroom with judge on bench and defendant standing, black and white
retiring clerk emptying his office desk into a cardboard box
wedding party in hazy soft focus and overexposed glow, dreamlike memory

name: Weak destiny
position_detail: secondary sign of composition (Deamer's division of Deleuze's 'destiny')
definition: Flashbacks that no longer determine the future but saturate present affects: ambiguous, incomplete, unmarked, perhaps belonging to several characters, the past is a clue to an ellipsis in the present that must be reconstructed before any future is possible.
deamer_quote: It is as if the past is a clue to an ellipsis in the present (p. 129)
deleuze_examples_note: None: Deleuze names only a general sign 'destiny'; the strong/weak split is Deamer's own, and Section II gives no films.

scenes: In the film's present Maria is stranded on a dirt track, then rides home in a rusty old bus while flashbacks unfold.
At night Maria shows new field workers bare concrete cells lit by a single torch, points out a water pump, and retires to her whitewashed villa.
The French army withdraws; gangs of youths take up arms and a child army invades the coffee plantation.
Maria finds a ram's bloody head as a warning, tries to hide it, and fails to wipe the blood from her hands.

operation: Slip into the past without a transition, let the flashback wander to other characters, and leave the present waiting in transit.
shot_criteria: A present-tense figure in suspended transit or waiting (road, bus, stranded), or an unanchored, unsignalled fragment of past violence/history that could belong to anyone; no clear optical flashback marker.
queries: woman standing alone on a dusty rural dirt road, waiting, wide shot
crowded old bus jolting along a dirt track, passengers seen inside
workers picking coffee berries on a hillside plantation
army trucks full of soldiers withdrawing down a country road
flashlight beam sweeping a bare concrete room at night
woman washing her hands in a basin as the water darkens, close up
colonial villa with white-columned veranda, servants carrying trays
armed teenage boys walking single file through tall grass

name: Forking paths
definition: Memory as fragmentation of linearity: flashbacks within flashbacks and circuits that fork within themselves 'like a split hair', exploring the past for itself as an inexplicable secret, so that psychological causality is exposed as a ruse.
deamer_quote: Flashbacks within flashbacks within flashbacks ... or irresolvable flashbacks (p. 130)
deleuze_examples: All About Eve (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1950)
A Letter to Three Wives (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1949)
The Barefoot Contessa (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1954) - forking multi-narrator flashbacks
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: In the ballroom of a ghost ocean liner, Jess aims a shotgun at another Jess as the camera circles the doppelgangers.
After a storm capsizes the yacht, survivors cling to the upturned hull until a liner emerges from the sea mist.
Jess studies her bruised body in a mirror and the camera passes through the glass to join her reflection.
Jess wakes washed up on a Miami beach on the morning before the trip, and the loop begins again.

operation: Build loops that fork within themselves: double the figure, pass through the mirror, and return to the start changed.
shot_criteria: A shot of doubling or looping: a figure and its double/reflection in the same frame, infinite mirror regress, multiple exposure of one person, a literal forking path, or the looping sea/ship imagery of the Section III scenes.
queries: woman at a mirror, her reflection repeated to infinity in facing mirrors
double exposure of the same man appearing twice in one room
large ocean liner emerging out of thick sea fog, wide shot
survivors clinging to a capsized sailboat hull in rough water
sailboat on a calm sunny sea, people sunbathing on deck
empty ballroom with chandeliers and overturned chairs
woman lying washed up on a beach at dawn, waves at her feet
footpath forking into two trails through a forest, seen from above

name: Mark
position_detail: first sign of full molar composition
definition: A habitual series of images, each interpretable by the others; perceived objects that repeat at least three times until the series forces itself into consciousness and becomes the chain of thought that constitutes the narration.
deamer_quote: there must be at least three such images to form a series (p. 133)
deleuze_examples: Hitchcock's relation-image generally (C1: 200-203)
Strangers on a Train (Alfred Hitchcock, 1951) - the exchanged crime as chain of relations
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: An obese man found bound and force-fed to death; 'gluttony' later found scraped in grease behind the fridge.
A lawyer's office with 'greed' written in blood on the floor and an upside-down picture hiding fingerprints.
A man tied to a bed for a year - the third murder that confirms the series (Sloth).
The Seven Deadly Sins listed in chalk on an old school blackboard, crossed off one by one.

operation: Repeat one kind of image three times so the audience starts reading every new shot as the next term.
shot_criteria: One visible term of a series: a numbered/listed item, one of several near-identical scenes or objects, or a repeated inscription; strongest if the frame itself shows repetition (rows, lists, sets of three).
queries: list of words chalked on a school blackboard, some crossed out
detectives examining a crime scene, body under a sheet on the floor
fingerprint card studied under a magnifying glass, close up
single word scrawled in paint on a wall, close up
row of identical suburban houses along a street, repeating to the horizon
identical bottles moving along a factory conveyor belt
lighter, flashlight and telephone laid out side by side on a table
calendar pages tearing off one by one as clock hands advance

name: Demark
definition: An aberration in an established habitual series: one term leaps outside the web or contradicts it, producing a shock that reorients the chain of thought and becomes the new question of the narration.
deamer_quote: any aberration in the series becomes significant. A shock (p. 134)
deleuze_examples: Foreign Correspondent (Alfred Hitchcock, 1940) - the windmill turning against the wind
North by Northwest (Alfred Hitchcock, 1959) - the crop-duster where there are no crops
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

section3.film: Doctor Who - The Day of the Doctor (Nick Hurran, 2013)
scenes: Gallifrey besieged by the Dalek army; the general exclaims at three Doctors appearing at once.
The unnamed War Doctor, the incarnation who refused the name, prepares the doomsday weapon The Moment.
The Tenth and Eleventh Doctors are brought to confront their hidden predecessor.
Buried (Deamer's other example): among three sets of things in the coffin, a snake enters and leaves - the demark.

operation: Set up a regular series, then let one term appear where it cannot belong.
shot_criteria: A regular series visible in frame with one element out of place (out of step, wrong color, wrong direction, missing, or an object/animal where it cannot belong); the shot must show both the norm and the aberration.
queries: column of marching soldiers with one man out of step
flock of white sheep with a single black sheep in the middle
row of windmills in a field, one stopped while the others turn
small crop-dusting plane flying low over an empty field toward a man on the road
snake crawling across a wooden floorboard, close up
wall of framed portraits in a row with one frame empty
blue police telephone box standing alone in an open field
row of identical mannequins with one real person standing still among them

name: Symbol
definition: An abstract relation carried by a concrete object: demarks extracted from different series coalesce in one thing, which becomes a node bearing various relations (or variations of one) and so expresses an idea, belief or concept.
deamer_quote: an object expressing ideas, beliefs, concepts (Fig. II.33, p. 135)
deleuze_examples: The 39 Steps (Alfred Hitchcock, 1935) - the handcuffs
Notorious (Alfred Hitchcock, 1946) - the key
Suspicion (Alfred Hitchcock, 1941) - the glowing glass of milk
deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Black screen, breathing, then a zippo flame reveals Paul Conroy buried alive in a wooden coffin.
Close-ups and extreme close-ups of sweat, blood and dirty fingernails, lit by lighter, mobile phone and torch in abstract patterns of light and dark.
A snake enters the coffin and leaves it again - a vertical element crossing a horizontal plane, the promise of a way out.
The coffin itself becomes the symbol, as if the character were placed inside Hitchcock's McGuffin (the package in the train's baggage rack).

operation: Isolate one concrete object and let every relation in the film pass through it.
shot_criteria: A single concrete object isolated and charged by framing or light (insert close-up, object in darkness, object as the centre of a composition), strong enough to carry meaning beyond its function.
queries: face lit only by a cigarette lighter flame in total darkness, extreme close up
plain wooden coffin lowered into a grave on ropes
brown paper package on a train compartment luggage rack, passengers below
hand gripping a telephone receiver in a dark room, close up
snake emerging from a hole in the earth, close up
pair of handcuffs lying on a table under a lamp, close up
key held up in a hand, dramatic side lighting, close up
flashlight beam in a cramped wooden box, dirty hands in the light
